What do you notice?
        Something that I noticed was how small the block of humans was compared to the other blocks. Especially how much bigger the bacteria block was, as it represents the mass of all of them on Earth. Bacteria aren’t that big, but they have way more mass on Earth than humans. However, I am not surprised that plants have the largest mass on Earth, as they are literally everywhere. If I look over at the man-made technology side, all the blocks are huge. Since they are all man-made, it shows how much we have created and put onto our world.
    
    What do you wonder?
        I wonder how humans were able to create so much mass, when we don’t have a lot of mass in the beginning. We’ve created the whole right side of the image, even though we’re just a tiny block compared to the larger and huge ones.
    
    How does this relate to you and your community?
        This graph can show that humans have a huge impact on Earth. The man-made technologies relate to house building, everyday roads, water bottles, buildings, floors, and so much more.     Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.

raw_comment:
Immediately, an observable factor of the graph is that humanity, being the most specific group, is placed outside the other boxes, where the proportion of humanity to any other box is absolutely diminutive. The classifications are also evident, with technomass and biomass being separated. Nonetheless, viruses also are kept nearly isolated, with it not being considered a living organism but not being a man-made entity. What I wonder is that, unlike humans, the virus is kept closer to the biomass side of the spectrum for a reason that I cannot understand. It is neither man made nor technology, so it should reside in between the two classifications. Regardless, humanity is apparently put in the middle even though they are living organisms, and viruses are visualized in the domain of life. On the contrary, the graph can illustrate a perceivable contrast between humanity and their creations, disclosing that the human community is outnumbered by their resources, and showing the advanced state of human technology. Currently, humans are swamped by substantial issues such as climate change and warfare, which can easily be explained by the amount of resources available for humans to commence such harrowing actions. 
    
    Catchy Headline: 
    Biomass outnumbered by Technomass, a New Revolution
    
    - Euntak Oh, TMS

raw_comment:
Headline: Man-Made vs. Living Stuff: What Makes Up Our Planet?
    This graph has different cubes representing the mass of multiple “living stuff” and “man-made stuff.” I think the purpose of this graph is to get readers to analyze and compare the different cubes. I notice that plants, concrete, and aggregates are the most enormous cubes, meaning they have the most mass on Earth. I also noticed that humans and viruses are the most miniature cubes, meaning they make up the least mass on the Earth. I also saw most of the cubes separated into two groups. One is “living stuff” on the left, and the other group is “man-made stuff” on the right. Viruses are close to the living stuff group but moved slightly away. The human cube is in between the two groups. I wonder why humans do not belong to the residing group. I also wonder what aggregates and asphalt are. I wonder about this because I have never heard of them; they seem to make up a lot of mass on Earth. This graph relates to me and my community because we make up part of this graph. We are a part of the human cube. In my community, we also witness the masses of other cubes. For example, we see plants, plastic, animals, metals, and bricks daily. This graph gives my community and me more awareness of our surroundings and the mass of different elements in the area.

raw_comment:
This graph compares the mass of different biological and technological forms worldwide. I first noticed in this graph that humans seem to have a smaller mass than viruses. This graph does a great job of representing just how big our world is. We think of viruses as so tiny, but humans are the tiny ones. I also noticed that the concrete mass is not much smaller than the mass of plants. I'd like to know what this graph would look like in twenty years. Would the concrete block get more prominent and the plant block get smaller? This affects my community because as technology increases, biological structures of society, such as plants, will likely decrease. This may lead to the destruction of the environment. It's essential to keep plants and other biological forms in mind due to their positive environmental impact.

raw_comment:
Thanks to all the students who responded.   There were so many great headlines, it was difficult to choose.  Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received:  
    
    "A Heavy Topic: Exploring How Man-Made Materials are Rapidly Overtaking Nature" by Azalea of Calif.
    "A Manufactured Earth: How Man-Made Objects Are Replacing Nature" by Deepak of Eaglecrest High School, Aurora, Colo.
    "Outweighed: How Human Made 'Stuff' Now Tips the Scale Against All Life on Earth" by Owen of Mass.
    "Humans Dwarfed by Their Own Creations: The Battle of Biomass vs. Man-Made Materials" by Blake of Gull Lake High School in Richland, Mich.
    “More Plastic Than Animals on Earth! A Graph that Compares Things Made by Man vs. Made by Mother Nature” by Olive and Sienna of Closter, NJ
    “Humans Are Small, But Our Footprint Is Massive” by Giulia Academy of Saint Elizabeth at Convent Station, N.J.
    “A Concrete Jungle—Literally! How We’ve Reshaped the Planet” by Johan Perth Amboy High School, N.J.
    "Man-Made Matter Now Outweighs Natural Life on Earth" by Rainelys of Perth Amboy High School, N.J.
    “Man-Made Masses: Is There a Weight Problem?” by Jayden of Tenakill Middle School, N.J.
    “The Mass of Civilization Outweighs the Mass of Nature” by Jordan of Great Neck North High School, N.Y.
    “Biomass vs. Technomass: The Story of How Human-Made Creations Surpassed Mother Nature” by Rachel of Holly Springs High School, N.C.
    "Humans Have Built More Than Nature Can Grow: The Rise of Technomass" by Will of Holly Springs, N.C.

raw_comment: I notice that plants (biological) make up the majority of the biomass on earth, as a part of the living organisms on earth. I also noticed that the mass amount of plastic is larger than the mass of humans, animals, and viruses. The humans have the smallest mass out of all of the categories. I wonder if these numbers have always been like this, with techno mass taking up more mass in the world than biomass, or if it was ever the other way around. In other words, I wonder if at any point in life biomass took up more mass than techno mass. It is interesting to see different people around the world who live in opposite conditions, where they are surrounded by farmland and lots of plants, with less manmade objects to rely on. raw_comment:
1. This graph shows the mass of different life forms and the mass of different man made materials on earth. I noticed that plants have the largest mass of living creatures, likely because of the large number of plants on earth. I was surprised that the mass of all bacteria is larger than that of animals and fungi. After researching, I found that there are approximately 5 nonillion bacteria in the world, explaining their mass. I noticed that humans have the smallest mass of the included life forms, which really puts into perspective how small we are. When it comes technological materials, the masses are more predictable. Concrete has the most mass, explained by its worldwide use in roads, parking lots, sidewalks and more. Comparing the two sides, I was surprised that plastics have more mass than animals.
    2. How was the mass of each category determined? Would this graph have looked different 20 years ago? What smaller categories were excluded form this graph? 
    3. This relates to me because I live among climate change and am watching nature slowly deteriorate while we continue to build structures in its place. This reality is reflected in the graph. 
    4. "Biology vs. Technology: How the Building Blocks of Our World Stack Up"

raw_comment:
Headline:
    Biology and Technology: How Two Forms of Mass Make Up Our World
    
    The graph depicts the mass of biological (living) forms and the mass of technological (man-made) forms on Earth. Each form is represented by a box, indicating its mass. The first thing I noticed when looking at this graph is that plants make up the largest mass in the biological forms. However, the technological mass in all still seems to outweigh the biological forms 1.3 trillion to 1.1 trillion. I also noticed how small the boxes of viruses and humans are compared to the other boxes. One thing I wonder about is when the technological forms started to outweigh the biological forms. Also, how would this graph look in the future, about 100 years from now? This relates to me and my community because it worries me about how the man-made forms outweigh the biological forms. As someone who lives on earth along with everyone else, I believe we should start practicing more sustainability and using less plastic and man-made materials. I also live in a more suburban area, across from the city and next to nature. This means I experience both the technological forms and biological forms.

raw_comment:
Headline: Humans Are Small, But Our Footprint Is Massive
    This graph shows the difference between the Earth’s mass of “living stuff” (biomass) and the Earth’s mass of “man-made stuff" (technomass). I noticed that there seems to be more techno-mass than bio-mass. The largest category of biomass is plants, while the largest category of technomass is concrete. Another big thing I noticed is that there is more plastic than animals, which is extremely concerning. It makes me wonder how this balance has changed over time and what it means for nature. What would this graph have looked like 100 or 1,000 years ago? How much have climate change and deforestation contributed to such low levels of biomass? This relates to my community because I now see so much more construction and roads than forests. Townhomes and buildings are being built day after day, reducing the forests and plants in my community by so much.

raw_comment:
I noticed that the graph depicts the mass ratio of living things such as plants and bacteria to the mass of man-made things like metals and concrete. Man-made substances seem to outnumber the nature in mass. On the living side, plants contribute the most in numbers, while on the man-made side concrete does. I also noticed that humans are very small in numbers compared to all the other categories in the graph. For the most part, metals and concrete are more dense then living substances. 
    I wonder how this information bout the mass of living things was obtained. There are many different types of plants that vary in mass. How did they get an estimate? Were all types of plants calculated? I also wonder if in the future, man-made objects will surpass living things in quantity, not just mass. 
    This relates to me and my community because I live in the Suburbs, where nature is prevalent. Many woods and swamps are near where I live, and there are efforts to conserve them, instead of building over them. 
    Catchy title: "Man v Nature"

What do you notice?
    I notice that the graph is showing man made materials and substances vs natural ones. The side of the manmade are very dark, and sad colors. In contrast, the natural materials and substances are colorful, and bringing life. I think this is due to the fact that the man made materials are harmful to the environment, and the natural one are not. I notice that there is more disease present then humans. In total, the mass of man made materials adds up to be more than natural ones.

    I wonder why we continue to create manmade materials to the point they are overtaking natural ones. Will these materials replace plants one day? I also wonder if the Size of the cubes represent the mass they take up on the world.

raw_comment: In this graph, I noticed that man-made mass is much larger than biomass on the Earth. In the biomass category, plants take up the most mass. In the man-made mass category, concrete takes up the most mass. I also noticed that humans were the smallest in comparison to every other recorded mass. For example, all the man-made mass was created by humans and is the largest part of our earthly mass. I am curious what would happen if the biomass categories were equal or larger than the man-mad mass. I also wonder what would happen if the man-made mass was smaller, and was there a period where it was smaller? Finally, I am curious if, in the next 10 years, this graph will change and man-made mass might become even larger. This relates a lot to my community because humans are constantly creating and changing the world around us. Knowing the components of our Earth and how they impact it is extremely important to taking care of the world.

raw_comment: This graph shows the amount of mass on Earth from two different categories: biomass and technomass. Firstly, I noticed how man-made mass outnumbers biological mass on the Earth. I also noticed that the biggest group for biomass is plants and the rest of the biomass categories are much smaller. Technomass does not have one category that is much larger than another; the categories are all relatively the same amount. I also noticed how humans are the smallest block, yet cause the most amount of mass despite their physical smallness. I wonder if there would be a beneficial impact on the world if biomass outweighed technomass and what the effects of that would be. This relates to my community and myself because it is scary to see how plastics, concrete, and bricks outweigh many of the natural things that come from our planet. A title could be: “Man vs. nature: who will win?”

raw_comment:
What I noticed...
    The graph shows Earth's biomass versus technomass. Plants dominate biomass, followed by bacteria, fungi, and tiny animals. Viruses are smallest. For technomass, aggregates and concrete lead, with bricks, asphalt, metals, and small plastics following. Humans appear as a minuscule dot, yet our created materials now outweigh all living things.
    What do you wonder...
    I wonder how fast technomass is growing versus biomass. When did this crossover happen? Do certain materials cause more environmental harm despite smaller mass? How have human activities changed biomass proportions over time, and what might future trends show?
    How does this relate to you and your community...
    On Cape Cod, this graph reflects our delicate balance between nature and development. Our marshes, beaches and forests represent vital biomass, while vacation homes and roads add to technomass. Rising seas threaten both, making our community especially vulnerable. Our local conservation efforts directly impact this global balance.
    Catchy headline for graph...
    "Outweighed: How Human Made 'Stuff' Now Tips the Scale Against All Life on Earth"

I notice that the mass of biological forms is significantly smaller than that of technological forms, with metals and asphalt having the most height compared to all other blocks. 
    
    I wonder if the mass of biological forms will remain approximately uniform going into the future. In contrast, technological mass will gradually increase over time due to the widespread use of technology and advancements. 
    
    This relates to my community and myself because it makes you think about how much of this mass you contribute to the total as a town or a state. raw_comment:
1. Humans clearly have the smallest amount out of all the other cubes. There is much more man-made cubes in sheer size and number, which really shows how much the humans have created over the years of our time existing on Earth. Even though humans have the smallest cube, they have created a lot, even more that biological things that were made.
    2. I'm wondering on how the graph can change based on what year it takes place, since humans need time to grow and make more things. I am sure that there was one point at which the biomass was larger than man-made objects.
    3. This can connect to me because it shows me just how much humans have created, like the areas I eat, go to school, and sleep. As the technology mass continues to grow, I am sure I will start to see changes around my town and it can come in different ways.
    4. Title: "How the production of man-made objects and technology have outweighed the amount of bio-mass in the Earth".

raw_comment:
Notices:
    I noticed that this visual representation shows that humans represent the minority, in comparison to the other categories present. Despite having over 8 billion humans, they remain the smallest group, emphasizing the immense quantities of other groups of biomass and techno mass. I also noticed that there is a larger quantity of techno mass than biomass, with more man-made than natural production. Lastly, I noticed there is a large quantity of micro-organisms, such as, bacteria, archaea, and protists. 
    Wonder:
    I am curious how animals, despite having millions of different species, have a smaller collective mass than most other masses, such as plastics. Unlike the other groups in this graph, the animal category is a collective mass across many different species of animals, instead of a specific organism or material. This leads me to wonder about the calculation process, as I am curious how this is tabulated. I am curious to see the accuracy of this visual, as it is extremely difficult to gather information of such vast quantities. 
    Relevance to my community:
    This is relevant to my community, as we might not see the bigger picture of biomass and techno mass, due to the fact that we live in a suburban area. We can't observe the magnitude of techno mass in comparison to biomass as much as a person living in an urbanized community, proving the relevance and importance of this illustration.
    Headline:
    "Man-Made Production Outweighs the Earth's Natural Production"

raw_comment:
Shown in the diagram, we notice that plants have slightly more mass compared to concrete. Fungi also has similar mass to plastics while bacteria also seem to have similar mass to bricks. Among the objects, the second smallest is viruses. However,  the smallest of all the masses are humans  at the bottom. This likely showcases how big these masses are. Hence, we are able to see at first sight that there are more technomass than biomass, thus most of the technomass seem to  outweigh every biomass. This is well-connected to our society as, almost anywhere we see, we spot more of technomass used or wasted than any biomass used. A possible headline that captures the graph's main idea would be:
    'Look Around You; Are There More of Technomass or Biomass?'

Notice: While looking at the graph, I noticed how us humans make up just a small amount of the Earth compared to the planet's biomass and technomass. Even viruses make up more of the planet than humans do. In biomass, The majority is made up of plants, quickly followed by bacteria and other microscopic organisms. In technomass, the majority is concrete, followed by aggregates and other man-made materials. On our planet, we assume that animals/plants/humans make up a lot more of the planet than man-made materials, but this graph proves otherwise, showing how much of the Earth isn't natural.

Notice: Some aspects of the graph I notice is that technomass, man made material, has a greater mass than biomass. I believe this is because humans use many man-made materials instead of natural, biodegradable materials. raw_comment:
Notices: I saw the graph was that it was a visual representation of the quantities of specific groups of living organisms and unnatural resources. I was surprised that animals were one of the minorities in the total biomass of the Earth. Despite each individual animal life form being significantly larger than bacteria, fungi, protists, and archaea, the animal collective mass makes up far less of the planetary total than one would assume.
    Wonder: I am curious as to how these totaled values were determined, and how accurate they are. If the entire human population was the smallest category on the graph, I would imagine it must have been very difficult to evaluate the biomass of  other categories such as all plant life on Earth. 
    Relevance: As a resident of a suburban area, it relates to my community because it is not so obvious that technomass outweighs biomass by such a large margin in the world. It is eye-opening to see the ratios in the graph, as it brings perspective to humanity’s place on Earth. 
    Potential Headline: “The Unexpected Difference in Living and Non-Living Items On Our Planet”.

raw_comment:
I noticed that in total, the mass of technological forms outweighs the mass of biological forms by a significant amount. I also notice that the largest biological form of mass is plants, and the largest technological form of mass is concrete. 
    I wonder what the major push factor was to create such high yields of technological mass and if that could be replicated in the future? I also wonder what negative impacts this may have on our environment and world as a whole?
    This relates to me and my community because it represents the industrial based world we are living in. The graph demonstrates that there is a greater demand for technological mass, which likely effects those who rely on biological forms to make a living, such as farmers. It also shows how communities are changing with growing populations. The large amount of materials such as metals and concretes leads me to believe that they are being used to build more housing and businesses, which effects the communities economy and way of life. 
    Title: Humans imbalance; more creation than creators

1. What do you notice?
    I noticed that this graph isn’t your normal graph; it was created in cubes. The amount of human-made materials is drastically higher than the amount of biological forms. There are fewer humans compared to animals and plants. 
    
    2. What do you wonder?
    I wonder why this graph was created in this way. How come man-made materials overshadowed the biological environment?

We need to know this type of thing, for us to be able to find a solution that could help us bring down the amount of man-made items in our environment.
    
    4. A catchy headline 
    “Visualizing the Imbalance: Human Impacts vs. Nature”

raw_comment:
1. I notice a large emphasis on the mass of techno mass over biomass, but the graph fails to explain what this means for the world. Some inferences can be made as to what this means, but it is mostly unclear, as the world is made mostly of rocks rather than organic material, so to me, it makes sense for there to be more techno mass than biomass. It is similar to comparing the Earth to all humans, which that difference is common sense.
    
    2. I wonder what exactly they are trying to portray here, as the techno mass is developed from construction, and construction leads to environmental problems. Maybe this is trying to show how much we rely on buildings and man-made structures.
    
    3. This relates to me and my community because we are surrounded by buildings every day. The houses we live in, cities with towering skyscrapers, and even the schools we learn in are all made by techno mass. Growth in techno mass shows infrastructure improvements, which would exemplify communal growth. However, the environmental impacts it may have may one day hurt the community rather than support it.
    
    Catchy Headline: The biggest manmade structure weighs more than the entire sum of the world's biomass

What do you notice? Provide evidence. 
    
    I notice that humans are incredibly miniscule in comparison to the other aspects of our world. It is a common thought that as humans we are the biggest issue, but this graph makes it evident that this isn't the case. Additionally, I notice that the amount of concrete and plants shown in the picture are about the same, which signifies that we are doing a good job of maintain our plant life despite construction. 
    
    What do you wonder?
    
    I wonder if these numbers and ratios are what is best for our Earth. If the amount of concrete to bacteria is not the way that would be best for us to sustain life to the highest quality, what needs to change, why is it bad, and how do we know it is bad? I would be interested to know how often and how quickly these numbers and ratios change as well. 
    
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    
    The things shown in this graph are the aspects that make up my day-to-day life and allow me to sustain life. This means that this graph allows me to be more mindful about the affect my actions (such as using plastic or planting a tree) might make on the world around me. My community is affected by the graph because it might show constructing workers what kind of materials to use or allow people to better educate themselves on what is happening in the world around us.

What do you notice? Provide evidence.
    I notice that as time goes on and on, more and more materials are used. Yes, our population has significantly grown, but the inorganic substances to organic substance ratio has changed substantially.
    
    What do you wonder?
    I wonder what changed in the mindset of humans to need more to survive. Before modern industrialism, humans survived with very little and no modern machines. However now, people can't even fathom the idea of living without these man-made products.
    
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    This relates to my community because living in a suburb, there are more man-made items than there is natural. Less than 50 years ago, Holly Springs, North Carolina was all farmland and now it is full of concrete buildings and corporations.
    
    Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
    A catchy headline for this graph could be: The weight of man-made objects, and how they weigh on nature.

1. The majority of the earth's biomass is plants. But, also a surprisingly large amount of those living things in our earth's mass are microorganisms.     the mass of civilization outweighs the mass of nature

raw_comment:
The average human made products seem to contribute more to the Earth's biomass than the natural features. Concrete measures at 661 gt, while plants measure 900. This may look like a big difference, but plants have been around for a much longer time than concrete, yet their sizes are close. wonder how accurate these numbers are. This relates to me because we are a part of the 0.12 gt that has created all of the plastics, asphalts, etc. These things did not naturally appear, but are very close to overtaking other natural parts of the Earth.
    
    "Could Concrete One Day Overtake Plants?"

One thing that I noticed is how things such as fungi take up more space than animals. When considering each factor that contributes to the global biomass, I initially believed that animals would take up more space than things such as fungi due to how large most animals can be in comparison to forms of fungi. When evaluating the website, fungi took up 24 gt while animals only took up 5.2 gt. 
    
    One thing I wonder is how certain animal classifications have grown to a higher extent than humans. With humans constantly discussing overpopulation, I found it interesting that humans took up so little space in comparison to smaller creatures such as arthropods, and I wonder how this came to be.
    
    This relates to me and my community as we're constantly surrounded by humans but not as much when regarding animal classifications such as arthropods, which made me underestimate the entire amount of space that they take up.

raw_comment: After looking at the biocubes, I notice most prominently that technomass now outweighs biomass, and the majority of the growth for technomass bas been since 1990, so the growth has been extreme within the last 34 years. I also notice how little animals contribute to biomass, let alone humans, yet we have created such a massive contribution that is inevitably affecting the world with technomass. With this being said I wonder what impacts this surge of technomass is having on the environment, and the natural biomass that makes up our world. I also wonder how we can control the surge of technomass and potentially bring down its impact. This relates to me and my community because I live in an actively developing town, surrounded by construction. I cannot leave my neighborhood without passing through some form of large construction, so we are actively contributing to the technomass. A headline for this graph could be: "Biomass: Outweighed by Human Creation."

raw_comment:
I noticed that out of all of the blocks that make up the biomass of our world, humans were a very small part of it. Humans were only "0.12 Gt" compared to the "900 Gt" of biomass for plants. I also noticed that the amount of concrete has increased significantly over time, totaling up to "661 Gt" in mass. I wonder why the use of concrete has increased more than the use of other resources. This relates to my community and me because as my community continues to develop, the need for resources will increase, plants will be destroyed to make room for buildings, and the number of people living in my community will increase. 
    
    A catchy title would be: How Heavy is the World?

raw_comment:
I notice that the use of building resources such as concrete, bricks, and aggregates began to pick up a lot of usage starting in 1950. The blocks were rising slowly and then picked up pace and grew exponentially from there. I noticed this was a similar pattern with all of the groups of blocks.
    I wonder if part of the reason technomasses outweigh biomass in our world is because they weigh so much more individually and are much more solid.
    This relates to me and my community because there is a lot of development in our town that is replacing forests and habitats in order to make way for more shops and homes.
    Weighed down by technomass

raw_comment:
Observations - This graph, in cubes, shows Earth’s biomass (left) and technomass (right). In terms of biomass, plants have the highest mass. Bacteria has the second highest, followed by fungi, archaea, protists, and animals. Next to viruses, humans have the lowest mass. Meanwhile, in terms of technomass, concrete has the highest amount followed by aggregates, bricks, and asphalt. Behind metals is plastic, which has the lowest amount. Comparing both sides, there is more technomass than biomass. 
    
    Questions - What factors have contributed to technomass surpassing biomass over time? How does the rise in technomass impact ecosystems and biodiversity? What are the environmental consequences of materials like concrete, bricks, and asphalt dominating Earth's mass?
    
    Relation to Community -  Acknowledging the growing amounts of technomass in NJ and understanding its trends would be instrumental in promoting more biologically-friendly actions to reduce the strain on the environment. 
    
    Headline - "Heavier Than Life: How Human Creations Tipped the Balance"

raw_comment:
What do I notice?
    I notice that the mass of plastic is likely 10x bigger or more than the mass of humans. The mass of concrete and asphalt is about the same as the mass of plants. I also noticed that most of the man-made materials are used for "ground" or buildings.
    
    What do I wonder?
    I wonder how the mass of bacteria is so large and where there are bacteria that we don’t even realize. Why is the ground we build so much greater than all of the nature surrounding us? Why do bacteria weigh so much more than viruses?
    
    How does this relate to my community?
    I think it makes sense that the weight of buildings, roads/sidewalks, and items used adds up to more than the untouched nature outside even in a small town. There could be an even more drastic difference for people living in very urban areas. It shows that what we do and make has more of an impact than our physical bodies. 
    
    Catchy Headline:
    Man-made vs Nature-made: You may be surprised by who wins

raw_comment:
What do I notice?
    I notice that the two groups seem similar in proportion to one another, with the industrial materials slightly taking the lead.  I also noticed that concrete makes up the bulk of the industrial substances, just as plants make the bulk of the natural substances.  I think this is cool, because both seem to be the structure that environments form around.
    
    What do I wonder?
    I wonder which aggregates make up the "aggregates" block, because concrete is primarily composed of aggregates, leaving only a few other aggregates left to be drawn from.  I also wonder what all the viruses in the world would look like if you combined them all in a collective cube, because I think that would be very interesting to see what color or texture the viruses would form when brought together.  
    
    This affects my community because I live in a place where farms are a regular sight, and being able to visualize just how large the biomass of plants and animals is compared to humans helps to demonstrate how few humans actually tend to the agricultural sectors of our societies, in relation to the organisms they are tending.  
    
    A Tale of Two Blocks:  The Battle Between Natural and Manufactured Resources on Modern Earth.

What do you notice?
    Something I noticed is how much bacteria we have on earth. It was also shocking to see that the amount of bacteria is very similar to the amount of brick we have on this earth. The amount of man made stuff outweighs the amount of human life we have on this earth which was something that surprised me. 
    
    What do you wonder?
    I wonder what the world will look like in fifty years with all the man made material we have on earth? I wonder how viruses outweigh humans and how they can decide that?
    
    How does this connect to you?
    This connects to me because my whole life I have lived around farms and woods that significantly exceeds that amount of man made materials around. 
    
    Heading:
    “Man Made vs Natural”

raw_comment:
A significant detail I noticed is that there is almost as much man-made brick mass as there is bacteria mass. I think that is very interesting considering how much brick there is and how large it is compared to usually invisible bacteria. I was surprised simply by how much bacteria mass there is on Earth. I also notice how little human mass there is. It is shocking to see how much man-made material there is compared to how many humans there are.

raw_comment:
I noticed that technological forms create the most mass when compared to living forms. Humans are notably low on this scale with 0.12GT and the largest mass being 661GT. Technological forms of mass production are about 1,300GT while biological ones are only 1,100GT, demonstrating that technological forms of mass are much more harmful to the Earth due to the greater mass being produced. 
    
    I wonder if there are cleaner ways to produce technological mass to better the environment. This way we can still provide people with stability in the community while keeping the Earth cleaner to ensure that resources and environmental health don’t deplete too celerity. I also wonder if there are materials that we can make out of plants so that not too many chemicals and masses are being produced that can harm the environment.
    
    In my community, many people plant trees and plants that better the environment. However, there are also many building and roads that are built in my neighborhood. With the uprising population, more building and means of transportation will be build meaning that the mass for technological forms will be produced. Overall this will harm the environment and eventually we may run out of resources.
    
    “Green or Machine: A Breakdown of Mass Sources”

raw_comment:
At first glance, I notice that plants have the largest biomass and concrete has the largest man made mass. I also see that viruses have a larger biomass than humans, which is surprising. Humans have the smallest total mass out of all the categories. Another surprising thing I notice is that there’s more plastic than animals on Earth.
    I really wonder why there are more viruses than humans because that doesn’t really make sense to me. I wonder why there’s so much concrete— almost enough to rival the biomass of plants. My biggest question is how protists, archaea, and bacteria could possibly weigh more than humans. They’re literally microscopic, so that must mean there’s an enormous amount of them on Earth. 
    This relates to me and my community because my generation will keep producing these man made materials until they weigh more than most of the bio forms. 
    Headline: Technological Forms Almost Larger Than Life
